header.author: Libanius
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg2200.tlg00446.opp-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00446.opp-gr: 1.2: 'the man who is ashamed to appear humane' renders τὸν εἰ φανεῖται φιλάνθρωπος ἐρυθριῶντα, literally 'the one blushing if he will appear humane'. 6.1: Aeacus is the proverbially just judge; Eurybatus a proverbial scoundrel. 8.1: 'ᾤμην γε τον' read as τοῦτον; 'that man' (ἐκεῖνος) appears to be Florentius' father; Tatianus' son is presumably Proculus. 13.1: 'μηδὲ δύ' ἄρχοντε πίνοντε' is obscure, perhaps corrupt; translated literally. 'Curator' renders λογιστής.

15.1: τηδείους read as ἐπιτηδείους ('friends'); 'the man ill spoken of is finished' (τὸ κακῶς ῥηθὲν πέπαυται) is uncertain and may rather mean 'the abuse stops'. 18.1 and 24.1: βάνειν read as λαμβάνειν. 18.4: τοὺς χοὐς is evidently corrupt; the context (eyes that do not see) shows τυφλούς, 'the blind'. 18.6: γοντος read as a form meaning the collector (ἀπαιτοῦντος or ἄγοντος). 18.4: 'having their breadth cleared through them' renders an obscure phrase about the drains. 27.1: τὰ ματα read as τὰ γράμματα ('the notices'). 28.1: γεις is a fragment of a verb (perhaps ἐλέγχεις, 'put to the proof'); the sense of the clause is uncertain.

§29: 'ὁ μὴ πον ὄνομα τιθέμενος' is corrupt; perhaps '[the bad] name'; rendered with [...]. 'Lesbos ... proverb' and 'Siphnos' allude to proverbs of sexual indecency (λεσβιάζειν, σιφνιάζειν). §30: 'him beside whom everything concerning us is lesser' presumably refers to the riot of 387; 'the Paeonian king' is unidentified and may be corrupt. §31: 'εἰκέστερα' read as 'ἐπιεικέστερα'. §38 is obscure and the text may be faulty; translated literally. §39: 'ἔπιθι λέγειν' is doubtful (perhaps a corruption of a verb for giving last instructions). §40: 'in that position' refers to the councillors standing on foot while the governor rode. §42: 'τὸ ἀρχόμενον' taken adverbially ('from the start'); the sense is uncertain.

Section 44 seems corrupt in several places. "Do the colonnades show the one who loves [us]?": the Greek of this question is obscure, and the rendering is tentative. "Of cold" translates κρύων, which makes little sense here; it may be a corruption, perhaps for a word meaning "tears" or "streams". The phrase "[the work of men who loved] themselves" supplies the sense the syntax seems to need. "Are shown one [kind of] respect" renders αἰδὼς δὲ μία literally; the sense expected is "there is no respect", so a reading such as οὐδὲ μία may lie behind it. "The price of the stones" is a tentative rendering of τὰ τῶν λίθων χρήματα.

nodes.text: It is nothing new, Emperor, that I have done in not visiting this man, who received so great an office in his youth, after I had made many trips to him. For I have come through many such changes, not because of my own badness but because of the badness of those who were unable to remain as they first showed themselves. And I am not ashamed to censure one whom I praised before, when I see that he has become someone else. The opposite would be shameful: if, when they had changed, I did not follow the facts but stayed the same toward one who was no longer the same.

And this is what has happened now. As long as I saw this Florentius gentle toward his subjects, I thought him excellent and worthy of praise. But when I saw him harsh and savage, and no different from those who pride themselves on such things, I thought it right to shun, with a blush, the man who is ashamed to appear humane.

3. Hear, Emperor, how this whole affair came about. The advocates arrived from Cilicia ahead of him. So I went to them and asked whether he remembered what Homer said about Odysseus, and what sort of man he was toward the Ithacans. They said, emphatically yes, and that he took no pleasure in either putting men in chains or flogging them. I was delighted to hear this, and prayed that he would be like this to the end, asking for the impossible, as I later realised. For at once he threw into chains one of the councillors of our household who was refuting the charges brought against him, although he had no lack of sureties; and when there are sureties, there is no imprisonment on minor charges, such as those were. When I begged him to release the man, he said, reluctantly, that he would release him. But having said so, he let him stay in chains, so that the man needed other help.

Next he dragged away from advocacy one of the reputable orators and sent him off to land-surveying, to suffer for it, because once, when pleading for those who had paid him a fee, he had left out nothing that he thought it useful to say. This is how he thought fit to use the powers of his office: against a man whom he could not otherwise harm, since he had no means, he used the judgement seat.

Then there was a capable man, of the highest intelligence, full of books, who had administered a great many things and, as no one else could have, had made the market better in every respect by his experience in such matters and by his justice. This man, when he was being insulted in the theatre by those who had sold themselves to his enemies, he betrayed to people dissolute in manners, in language and in conduct contrary to the laws. Yet he ought to have followed the example of reputable governors, arrested some of the insulters, shown his anger, and punished the insolence of people kept by the prostitution of dancers, and not thought slanders more credible than deeds. And even if there was some justice in what was said against the man, the theatre was not the place for such claims of justice: we know where such things are examined. Those who had brought suit for this ought to have proceeded to the proof, and if they showed wrongdoing, he should have thought the convicted man bad; but if they had lied, he should in turn have demanded the penalty for false accusation.

But he, on bare accusations, took them for Aeacuses and the man for a Eurybatus, and without summoning, questioning or judging him, he drove from his post the best of the members of the council, a man whom he had earlier made his friend, passing over many others, and knowing that his own father too was on familiar terms with this councillor. Florentius, respecting none of this, flattered the rabble of the populace, and voted for them whatever they wished.

7. This too, then, advised me to look on the man from a distance and to count association with one who had neglected virtue as a loss; but he added to these some other things that gave the same advice. For he had these wretched people who live by buying and selling goods rounded up by the lictors (and each arrest was made a source of gain for each of the lictors, for if the arrested did not submit to this, they would have been throttled), and then, having spent the night considering what those held should suffer, he made the day a day of blows, as many blows on each as could be delivered by fifteen young men, with each man who tired bringing in his successor. For he thought, as his father had too, that those being beaten had backs of iron.

And that man was the first who dared to cause death by blows; he had Tatianus as his pupil, and Tatianus had his son. And I thought this man would be ashamed of their doings and would follow neither of them, nor become a beast instead of a man; but it seems he thought he had not even become a governor unless he did such things. Doctors' assistants, summoned to them by the relatives of each victim, seeing the pits dug in their bodies by the whips, recoiled, as having nothing adequate [to treat them]. And it was then that the admirable man thought he was truly governing, when he learned this. For he thought it shameful, it seems, to be humane, and to be called so, under you.

Shall we not, then, call this man a murderer, through whom some have perished, because he did not do it with a sword? But this is the very thing that is more terrible. For who among those led to death would not choose to die by that way rather than this? Everyone would, unless someone thinks the drawn-out time under blows lighter than a single swift stroke. I, for my part, think even highwaymen who kill with the sword more moderate than those who kill by long-drawn agonies. And let him who kills those whom the law hands over, and does not think himself a murderer because it was not with iron, know that he wrongs the law doubly, both by depriving them of life and by a more painful method. The Romans are better than the Persians in many other respects, and also in having devised a manner of death that is swift and not drawn out over a long time. But you, who have destroyed with blows a man whom you did not kill with the sword, say that you are clean? And who will tolerate it?

10. "For the tavern-keepers," he says, "were cheating the drinkers in the measures." Yes, Emperor, but they themselves were being wronged by the drinkers, not by all, but by not a few. Now if they did wrong without being wronged, they deserved punishment; but if they did harm because they were suffering harm, who would not forgive them? For this was not the act of men who wanted to, but of men compelled. And those who have an excuse and something to plead in their defence should not be put to death.

Do you want to learn, then, Emperor, how they are wronged? The offices are many, and in each there is a troop [of staff], and again in each of these there are heralds, couriers, torturers, and there are also some other functions that produce titles. These, being a multitude, burst into the taverns many times each day and drink as much as would make them drunk, not wine only but also what is mixed with it. And nobody counts the cups, not husband, not wife, not son, not daughter; they must either keep silent or be ruined. For they say they are using their own and are masters both of the jars and of those to whom the jars belong.

The more decent of them put down the cup, announce that they will look around for better wine, and leave; the others leave cups and all. Not an obol from either; the tavern-keeper buys, and they fill themselves up paying nothing. Then some have gone, and others have come. And the fear of those who drink for free must take precedence over those who pay. With the purse not staying put, the drinking is heavy. And a man does not drink alone, but also whoever he brings in, now a relative, now an acquaintance.

Count these up, Emperor: those under the governor of the province, those under the governor of more [provinces], those under the general, and do not leave out even the two officials who drink, for whom the workshops are almost all their farms. For they take from what each sells, the advocate joining the curator. And what do you think of the company of soldiers stationed there? Are they content with the rations from you? And who does not know of the plundering, which the seller does not try to stop, lest he provoke them, but begs to be less? These soldiers simply go at everything, dragging things off from all sides, and if there is no meat or anything of that sort, carrying off money.

And it is not only the fighting men who collect, but also those whose living lies in making the soldiers laugh. To reduce the property of the poor wretches, a tame lion is enough, and a bear and a leopard and a dog of exceptional size, and by now even an ape. One man plays the pipe and exacts payment, another comes with panpipes, another dresses himself up as Pan, another as Silenus, and someone else as a Bacchant. And if none of these is to hand, a horn suffices, its lip decorated with silver.

What comes under a still greater compulsion of giving is the informer and his people, the ears and eyes. And to the most blameless man every fault is imputed if the informer wishes it. Even if he is moderate, he is insolent. And to refute the charges, however easy that may be, he is not allowed to speak. Those who wish to entertain their friends at a Sybaritic table but do not care to spend become hosts at the cost of other people's misfortunes. Then some have their lunch, and others go back home, bringing their wives the knives and the story of the fear that forces everything.

This ought to have stopped at the informer, but as it is everyone who has any position whatever in the palace thinks he too should enjoy the same privileges, being more moderate than the informers only in so far as they say they will pay, even if the promises are false. And over these things I know of many wounds and tears, for the alley by the council-chamber teaches me this. At any rate many speeches have been interrupted by the wailing of those being beaten. What wonder then if, because of thefts of this kind, they did something with their weights such as they would not have done had they not been suffering this?

17. But here at least there are military cloaks and trousers and the name of the enemy, even if there is no love of danger; but these drones, who could bear the bellies of men who in idleness eat up the hardship of others? Whom do I mean? Those whose one task is to chant the acclamations of the rulers in the theatres. For in the theatres they have their strength, holding mastery over the market people through the power of their voices. And this tribe hurls thunderbolts at whomever they wish: they have shouted and they have persuaded, and the others are in trouble. And the man ill spoken of is finished. So one must either bow down to them or be ruined.

And what does bowing down mean? They ask, they receive; again they ask, again they receive, either sending men to do it or approaching in person. And if anyone pleads poverty as his reason for not lending, he gives offence; and for these offended men the revenge is in the theatres. And those [shops] are thrown open to many. And soldiers run about putting out fires, scattering firewood, letting nothing stay, overturning everything. Who could bear four hundred wolves? How is it possible, Emperor, both to serve these men and to disturb nothing of the rest? For the man who demands that both happen acts much like one who robs a person of both feet and orders him to walk.

19. But these things someone might even deny; that other thing, however, he cannot, since the facts cry it aloud. A lodging was appointed for those who travel on horseback, whether a long or a short way. This lodging, I suppose, needs couches spread, tables, cups on them, cooks, men to take off shoes, men to wash feet, men to bring prostitutes, and doctors if need be. All these things and still more, who are the ones who provide them? These men who are flogged. And if [a guest] breaks any of these things, or someone steals something, the same men must be the suppliers. And many of the servants, falling foul of the unjust anger of those lodging there, have died, and one must save oneself by persuading their parents with money. This lodging, Emperor, was built against the tavern-keepers, and whatever the tavern brings in, the greater part of it has gone there. For besides everything else, claiming to have been robbed when they have suffered nothing of the kind, they go after the tavern-keepers through hirelings and shake them down.

20. Now is the time, Emperor, to mention here what happens at the successions of generals. What then is the damage? Empty counters, empty jars. The man who has left office sells things that he too acquired by similar plunder, and the man who has taken over the office acquires them, looking to the day on which he too will sell them off.

21. To these I would not add the help given to the blind, often many times each month; for even if this too is a matter of expense, it is voluntary and brings pleasure to those who give. For they do not curse those who receive, but rejoice as they give with their own right hands that see, so to speak, into theirs that do not see and therefore wander. These, then, I do not count, nor did they ever; but who does not know that new columns put up in place of old ones are installed to the harm of these men, or with heavier hauling? For both fall to them, and either they must transfer themselves from their crafts to that work, or, keeping to their crafts, get it done for pay. And much harder than this are the drains, having their breadth cleared through them. Not a few of those who go down alive are drawn up dead, and the man who does not wish to perish has to run the risk in another's body, again a body hired for pay.

22. Let then that be spoken of too which has surpassed all the rest. This is the unbearable tax, the silver and gold, which makes the dread five-year periods a cause of shuddering as they approach. For this levy has a respectable name from the merchants, but while they use the sea to slip away, those whose hands barely bring them bread are ruined. Not even the cobbler escapes. I have often seen them raising the awl to heaven, swearing that in it lay all they had. Yet this does not rid them of those who press upon them, barking and all but biting.

23. This season, Emperor, increases slavery, driving out of freedom those who are sold by their parents, not so that the box may take in the price for them, but so that they may see it going into the hand of the collector. And let no one suppose that I am saying they should not collect at all, when war needs money, by which it is possible both to defeat enemies and to save subjects; but that those who pay must consider from what source they could pay. And the collector ought to be able to overlook something, so making those under pressure able to pay; for the man who twists and tortures beyond measure does this to the detriment of the tax. But one must not, Emperor, care so greatly for the very hungry as to take more thought for them than for the sinews of war.

Here, then, since the exchange is of this kind, nothing should be changed; but the other damages are not to be overlooked. Of these you will find the one now to be described the most unjust. For how is it just that officials, paying half the price, should feast, and the rich man take the poor man's goods, and the man he was appointed to make more prosperous he should make more wretched, and turn what comes from you to his own estate, while eating the flesh of the market people, and sleeping after such a dinner, and inviting friends to what belongs to others?

Then for such brigandage and wickedness they changed the name to 'service', as though by this they would take away something of the harm from those harmed, just as if someone were to call adultery friendship. And when they inquire of the cooks about these takings they do not sink into the ground for shame. Yet if someone indicted a private person who wanted to make these gains and proved it, what cries the judge would have let out, calling the thing tyranny! Nevertheless, daring to commit wrongs for which they would exact punishment, they claim to bring others to their senses.

26. What then, Emperor, is shown by all that I have said? That this fine fellow, who has so often seen the Tiber and drunk from the springs in Rome, ought not to have laid hands on the measures before rescuing the tavern-keepers from the raids. He should have summoned them and learned, as they lamented, of the invasions, not against the vines, as the Spartans did, but against the wine itself and the jars. As it is, what was just, to stop the damage and then call the tavern-keepers to account, he let go, and dropping the first went on to the second.

A thing easy to say: beat, and let another do the same, and a third and a fourth and a fifth, and so make the harm the work of fifteen arms. He should have posted notices and forewarned them not to do what they are now doing, then some days later summon again those who had been plundered and learn what the time after the notices had been like for them, and whether any of the outrages had been corrected, and in this way demand exact standards and regard them as wicked if, no longer being ill-treated, they did wrong.

But you, allowing those who despise the laws to do wrong in safety, while those not permitted to honour justice you put to the proof, add to justice and nature the weight of compulsion; and on the same day came both the blows and the wrongs of the drinkers. Among these were the very men who had done the flogging, coming in to similar cups. And the wives of the one lot lamented, while the others ordered [wine] poured again. So the blows had no rationale for you; for since you had neither helped them nor made them better, you had no reasonable ground for indignation.

29. But the whips were only a prelude for you. For in accusing, he says, the man was defending himself, and when called to account for what had caused the shouts he described the character of those who had shouted: that there were seditious men among them who drag along even those who know how to behave. And what is terrible in speaking about those who bring in these disturbances? You asked, 'Where does the faction come from?' They answered, 'From those who delight in faction.' For if you had asked someone how Ilium was taken, you would have heard of the valour of those who campaigned against it; and if how Sparta won renown, you would have heard of the laws and Lycurgus; and why Xerxes was content if he got away safe, of the Athenians and their navy. And if someone said about Lesbos what the proverb says, must he be beaten? And about Siphnos, would rods be needed? So now too it was not possible to praise those who behaved in a disorderly way and spoiled the pleasure of the theatre as having watched in good order. It was not, then, this man who gave [them] the name [...], but it arose from the facts themselves.

30. I would have wished, Emperor, that the city had the better reputation from everyone; but by no art could it escape this, the appearance of falling into factions. Nor could anyone erase Domitianus or Theophilus, or him beside whom everything concerning us is lesser. Through him you have become more illustrious, while we have been harmed in reputation, and we owe thanks that the city was not razed. And the Paeonian king who maltreated the many with many blows, in what reputation did he hold the crowd? Was it not the one that comes from disorder?

Those who regard the dancers as a calamity for the city, through whom many are idle, many profligate, many beat their fathers, and many count themselves fortunate if they are assigned to stand at the doors and do the tasks of slaves, those, then, who call the enthusiasm for them, from which come the foul cries, a sore of the city: have they taken the more lenient view of them or the harsher? I for my part think the latter. How then did this ruin the tavern-keeper? Or is there some law that forbids only a tavern-keeper to censure what is bad?

32. I wonder whether Florentius, who himself calls the commotion of that time a faction, thinks the man erred in his choice of word when he said that those who shrank from nothing in the theatre then were factious. Had he praised them, he would have had no argument, but would have been convicted; in accusing them, there was some hope. Did you then expect the man to become his own betrayer, so that none of those who had outraged the city should hear the truth spoken against him?

33. And what is new in a defendant accusing, and a man on trial bringing charges? Already a helmsman, too, who had woken a sailor with a wound, when brought to trial had one defence, the accusation, and this: 'For he was not rowing, and the oar was doing no work at all; his hand lay idly on the handle, and the oar merely followed the ship, while he snored, contributing nothing.' This would have been the helmsman's defence.

And a general, too, has before now caught a cowardly soldier of his making some of the others worse and like himself, and put him to death. And this man, when tried, would pour out a flood against the dead man, speaking of his complexion, his fear, his trembling, his doing nothing, his hindering the others, his cheering the enemy, his being an obstacle, and that his death had become an encouragement to the others. Who would have blamed the general defending himself in this way? Who would not have approved the killing? Who would not have said that there was force in what was said? And yet what is this other than accusation?

How could Orestes, who had killed his mother, have defended himself better than by accusing Clytemnestra of having confounded the rights of marriage, preferring a licentious youth to such a husband, and adding murder to adultery, as if Agamemnon owed a penalty for what he had suffered? And yet what greater thing could anyone say of that defence than that it seemed right even to gods sitting as judges?

But you wanted the tavern-keeper to look for a better defence than this? What kind? Where would it come from? He, then, began with the only defence there was, while you, instead of hating those who had chosen to be bad, thought that the man who could say nothing good about them ought not to exist. For he survives by the goodwill of the gods, but the number of hands did not intend this.

37. 'For it seemed terrible to me,' he says, 'that a whole city should be spoken ill of by a tavern-keeper.' But if this was true, it ought rather to have seemed terrible that a whole city should do wrong than that someone should find fault with a city. For the harm lies more in doing what ought not to be done than in there being someone who says so. Moreover, he did not even say that the blame belonged to the whole city, since he spoke not about everyone but about those in the theatre. For those absent far outnumbered those present, and the part that goes to the theatre is a tiny fraction of the part that does not see it, so that someone coming from elsewhere and seeing the city for the first time in the form of those seated together to watch what is on the stage would not reasonably say that he had come to a populous city. So even if the word had been said against all those in the theatre, it had not been said against the whole city.

They say too that he clearly absolved the greater part from the charge by saying 'some'. For he said that these were the doings of some who live in disorder. And indeed the man arrested at night was among those convicted, and wept. Thus what had not been said about the worthless had [in effect] been said. For he was neither seen by the judge nor questioned, so that he would have been among those things that happened even if he had kept silent, on the matter of the measures. For the blows were going to show the anger on account of which he had been seized.

That it would have turned out so, the following is the greatest sign. Those who had neither set [anything] nor given any answer paid fees to doctors on their own behalf, met with the same laments, and said to their wives and children 'go on to speak', their end being expected. But, I think, flattering the bad portion of those in the city, and regarding the acclamations of the worst as proof of the best rule, so that they might shout such things, he says he is vexed on their behalf and kills the man who does not think them some kind of equals of the gods.

'And indeed I love the city,' he says. Very much so, as he showed by his slighting of the council, putting a stade's distance between himself and their greeting, and not bringing himself to do the same as many noble prefects, who, whenever they saw the council in that position, leapt very nimbly into the hands of those who would set them on the ground; and nothing at all held them up aloft, not rain, not snow, not mud, not the crash of thunder, not the flash of lightning, not, the greatest thing, shadows of feet in place of feet wasted away by gout.

It is not the act of one who loves us, it is not, what has been done about the racehorses against the law that releases them from labour to enjoyment of the grass, for which the season gives the horses a craving, but you a deprivation, from which comes ruin. Hence poverty for the man performing the liturgy, and the community feels the loss suffered by the part.

It would have been the act of one who loves [us] not to make the court, from the start, harsher than reefs for those with lawsuits. For who could bear the mouths of so many attendants, surpassing those of wolves? With all of them demanding to receive, nothing moderate sufficing, and always more being sought, none of the limits fixed long ago remains; and those needing a verdict have been swamped both by the madness for gain of those through whom they pass, and by the chief of the robbers, who has turned one into four, so that those who go away full of staters praise him with their hand, while the man who needs his cloak for this nonetheless goes away thirsty. And you seem to have a share in the collection; for you would not tolerate so great an evil if there were no partnership.

43. Such is our educator of tavern-keepers, who sees the small things but does not want [to see] the greater. And if he had been unaware of the impiety in these matters, even so he would have been at fault in not knowing what was fitting, but there would perhaps have been some room for pardon; as it is, there are those who spoke to him and described it and urged him to take thought for himself and to help the court, saying that those who seize hold of people who come here for lawsuits, both when about to contend and after the verdict, are crueller than the evildoers in the wildernesses. And he, hearing this, invents a tale so implausible that it would not take in even a child, and says that this is not his doing but that of those who have ordered it.

But I would not have accepted this argument even against Aristides son of Lysimachus, and this man blames a compulsion that does not exist. For not even that man would have tolerated such a report. Surely he would have said: "But does he intend to act? Do the colonnades show the one who loves [us]?" But not even the earlier ones were the work of those who loved the city; [they were the work of men who loved] themselves, since each colonnade became a spring of gold, and the same one also of cold. For the first step in [building] colonnades is the demolition of houses that had sheltered many generations, so that, instead of a dwelling, their owners got the price of the stones. The same reckoning leads this man too to these things. And the word is that he will make the road wider by means of a colonnade; then, so that it may become a palm's breadth wider, every tomb has been laid bare, every grave outraged, and the bones of those who once lived in the city scattered, and the dead of good men are shown one [kind of] respect.

45. But resist this, O emperor: pity those who lie [in their graves], and preserve for each his last resting place. For perhaps it is not even safe to make so many souls into enemies of the city, and to make them hostile, to some as those who have wronged them, to others as those who have neglected them.
